title: What do we get when the folded strip is folded again?
description: A strip already folded into two equal parts is folded again, giving four equal parts. The length of one, two, three and four of the new parts is named. Keeko's doubt, that each part is one third because there are three creases, is broken.
teaching_notes: One idea: folding each half again makes four equal parts, and counting parts in that unit gives two fourths, three fourths and four fourths. Watch for students who count the creases instead of the parts.

source: What will you get if you fold the previously-folded strip again into two equal parts? You will now get four equal parts. 2 times 1/4 = 2/4, 3 times 1/4 = 3/4, 4 times 1/4 = 4/4.
video_script.why: The child folds each half again to get four equal parts, names one part, and then counts one, two, three and four of those parts.
video_script.substitution: Fold each half of the strip in two, then name the length of one new part and count parts from the left end.
video_script.anchor: A paper strip one unit long, already folded into two equal parts, folded once more
video_script.wrong_answer: each part is one third because there are three creases
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko counts the three creases and says each part is one third. Counting the spaces between the ends and the creases gives four equal parts, so the bubble is struck.
video_script.payoff_line: Each new part is one fourth of a unit long

final_answer.spoken: one fourth, two fourths, three fourths and four fourths of a unit

video_script.fraction_reading: one half, one fourth, two fourths, three fourths, four fourths, one third
never_show: 1/3 as the length of one part
maths_rules: the strip is 1 unit long; one fold gives 2 equal parts of 1/2 unit
folding again splits each half into 2 equal parts: 2 x 2 = 4 equal parts
1 unit in 4 equal parts: each part is 1/4 unit
1 part = 1/4; 2 parts = 2 x 1/4 = 2/4; 3 parts = 3 x 1/4 = 3/4; 4 parts = 4 x 1/4 = 4/4, the whole strip
slip: the strip shows 3 creases but 4 parts; counting creases gives the wrong unit
video_script.design: One idea: fold again to make a part of one fourth, then count parts in that unit. Assumes one half from the last video. Wrong idea: counting creases, not parts. The strip stays on the board to the end.

<bookmark mark='strip'/>The strip is one unit long and is already folded into two equal parts.
<bookmark mark='fold'/>We fold the folded strip again into two equal parts.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>What do we get, and how long are one, two, three and four of the new parts?

beats.on_screen: the strip holds still and the question stays on the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: the strip is drawn as a long bar of one unit with its middle crease; the two halves are marked 1/2 each

marks.halves: the middle crease splits the bar into two halves of equal length

beats.colours: the strip = amber, the halves = teal
narration: <bookmark mark='unit'/>The strip is one whole unit long.
<bookmark mark='halves'/>The first fold made two equal parts, and each part is one half of a unit.

beats.on_screen: Given: a strip of 1 unit with 2 equal parts, each part folded again into 2

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, a strip of one unit with two equal parts, and each part is folded again into two.

beats.on_screen: To find: how many new parts, and the length of 1, 2, 3 and 4 of them

marks.find: the words how many new parts and their lengths are written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find how many new parts there are, and their lengths.

beats.on_screen: Step 1: each half is folded into 2, so 2 x 2 = 4 equal parts

marks.fold: each half of the strip is folded into two equal parts
marks.four: the opened strip shows four equal parts

narration: <bookmark mark='fold'/>Step one, fold each half of the strip into two equal parts.
<bookmark mark='four'/>Two halves with two parts each give two times two, which is four equal parts.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: 1 unit shared into 4 equal parts; one part is one of the 4 equal parts

marks.share: one part of the strip lights up while the other three stay dim

narration: <bookmark mark='share'/>Step two, name one new part. One unit is shared into four equal parts, the same way as the roti shared among four children.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: count parts from the left end: 1 part, 2 parts, 3 parts, 4 parts = the whole strip

marks.count: the parts are counted one by one from the left end
marks.whole: the fourth part reaches the right end, and the four parts together make the whole strip

narration: <bookmark mark='count'/>Step three, count the parts from the left end, one part, two parts, three parts and four parts.
<bookmark mark='whole'/>Four parts reach the right end, so together they make the whole strip.

marks.list: the four lengths are written in a row

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Each new part is one fourth of a unit long.
<bookmark mark='list'/>Two parts are two times one fourth, which is two fourths. Three parts are three fourths, and four parts are four fourths, the whole strip.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the boxed answer
narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's doubt in a bubble; the strip shows 3 creases and 4 spaces between the ends and the creases, which are counted; the bubble is struck through

marks.fix: the spaces between the ends and the creases are counted as four, and the bubble is struck through
marks.spaces: the spaces are circled and the creases are crossed out

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks each part is one third because there are three creases.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>But the parts are the spaces between the ends and the creases, and there are four of them.
<bookmark mark='spaces'/>We count the parts, not the creases. Four equal parts give a unit of one fourth.
